rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a green shore crab, a review lists your sharpness at about half a cycle a degree, a sixtieth of the 30 cycles a degree a human reads on an eye chart. If you are a horned ghost crab, the same review lists under 2 cycles a degree, about a twentieth of a human's. Nobody has measured how sharply you see if you are a Dungeness crab, a Sally Lightfoot crab or a northern kelp crab, among many others.
rows.note: Left out the blue crab's 1.8 degree figure (R30) because it is an angle, and no record converts it to cycles a degree. Rounded the horned ghost crab's 1.57 to "under 2".

rows.title: The horizon
rows.text: If you are a horned ghost crab, a band across each eye level with the horizon is about 30 degrees high, and at its finest your eye samples four times more finely up and down than side to side. The fiddler crab Uca lactea has a band like this too, running around the middle of its eyes. Nobody has measured whether you have one unless you are one of those crabs or a close relative of the ghost crab.
rows.note: Left out the mantis shrimp records (not crabs) and R4, whose quoted value does not state a horizon band.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: The Asian shore crab has two kinds of color-sensing pigment in its eyes, one for violet-blue light and one for blue-green light, and you very likely have two as well. A review lists two kinds in the red swamp crawfish too. In the larger light-sensing cells of four fiddler crab species, only one kind was found.

cites.taxon: Uca pugnax, U. pugilator, U. vomeris, U. tangeri

rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "lists" for the voice check. Left out the crawfish peak numbers because the table gives "560/600" without explaining it.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: The shore crab Hemigrapsus sanguineus has one kind of color-sensing cell that peaks in violet-blue light, at about 440 nanometers, and one that peaks in green, at about 510. Four fiddler crab species have a single kind of cell, peaking between 510 and 530. Nobody has measured whether you have a cell that senses ultraviolet, the light just beyond violet.

cites.taxon: Uca pugnax, U. pugilator, U. vomeris, U. tangeri

rows.note: No record gives a crab cell peaking below 400 nm, so the row states the gap. Mantis shrimp UV records (R4, R13) left out because they are not crabs.

rows.title: Pace
rows.text: Nobody has measured how fast a light can flash before you stop seeing it flicker, and that is true for most crabs. If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes follow a flicker of about 75 flashes a second by day and about 60 at night, where a human stops at about 60. A review lists 14 flashes a second for the deep-sea crab Bathynectes longipes.
rows.note: No flicker measurement exists in the records for the commonly met crabs, so the row names only two measured crabs.

rows.title: Night
rows.text: If you are a Dampier's fiddler crab, your eyes are far more sensitive at night, and the dimmest flash that gives an electrical signal from your eye is about a thousand times dimmer than the one needed by day. Nobody has measured how dim a light you can see if you are most other crabs, crayfish or shrimp.
rows.note: Left out R2 and R3: their figures are calculated from eye dimensions in other species, and numbers do not travel.

rows.title: Crayfish
rows.text: Nobody has recorded what kind of eye you have if you are a red swamp crawfish, a signal crayfish or a yabby. A review says that many adult crabs keep apposition eyes, and an anatomical study found that slipper lobsters have a superposition eye with square facets. Nobody has checked whether a crayfish eye matches either one.
rows.note: Replaced "reports" with "says". R1's value text mentions reflecting eyes in shrimps, but its quote does not state it, so I left it out.

rows.title: Polarized light
rows.text: Polarized light is light whose waves vibrate in one direction, and fiddler crabs, mantis shrimp and the tawny hermit crab have all been shown to see it. The tawny hermit crab and two other hermit crabs spotted predator-like shapes by polarization contrast alone. If you are not one of the crabs that were tested, nobody has measured whether you see it.

cites.taxon: Coenobita rugosus and two other hermit crabs

rows.note: Left out the common mud crab result (R5, gaze steadied by brightness cues) and the signal crayfish anatomy (R7, suggestion only).
